summary: Ethionamide is a second-line thioamide antitubercular drug used as part of multidrug regimens for active tuberculosis, particularly multidrug-resistant TB, when first-line agents cannot be used. It is structurally related to isoniazid. It is poorly tolerated, with prominent gastrointestinal effects, hepatotoxicity, hypothyroidism, and neurotoxicity, and is always combined with other antitubercular drugs plus pyridoxine.
indications: Treatment of active tuberculosis, in combination with other antitubercular agents, when first-line therapy has failed or is not tolerated (including drug-resistant/MDR-TB)

dosage.d: 15-20 mg/kg/day (max 1 g/day); typically 250 mg 2-3 times daily, titrated up
dosage.n: Start low and titrate to improve tolerance; give with food
Weight-based; always combined with other agents

admin: Always use in combination with other antitubercular drugs - never as monotherapy
Give with meals or at bedtime to minimise gastrointestinal upset
Co-administer pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to reduce neurotoxicity
Titrate the dose upward gradually for tolerability
moa: Ethionamide is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial enzyme EthA; the active form inhibits InhA (enoyl-acyl carrier protein reductase), blocking mycolic acid synthesis essential for the mycobacterial cell wall. This mechanism is similar to isoniazid, and cross-resistance can occur.

relative: Diabetes mellitus (harder glycaemic control, retinopathy risk)

preg: Avoid in pregnancy - teratogenic in animal studies. Reserve for multidrug-resistant TB when no safer effective alternative exists, with specialist input and informed consent.
lact: Limited data on breast milk transfer; use with caution and weigh the benefit of treating maternal TB against potential infant exposure.
renal: Use with caution in renal impairment; dose reduction may be considered in severe impairment. Follow MDR-TB protocols for adjustment.
hepatic: Hepatotoxic and contraindicated in severe hepatic impairment. Monitor liver function tests before and during treatment; discontinue if transaminases rise significantly or jaundice develops.

major: Other hepatotoxic drugs including some antitubercular agents (additive liver injury)
moderate: Isoniazid (additive neurotoxicity and hepatotoxicity; potential cross-resistance)
interactions.food: Take with food to reduce GI intolerance
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - increased risk of psychotic reactions and hepatotoxicity
interactions.diagnostics: May elevate liver enzymes, alter blood glucose, and raise TSH (hypothyroidism)

monitoring: Liver function tests before and periodically during therapy
counsel: Take with food or at bedtime to reduce nausea

Report yellowing of skin/eyes, severe mood changes, vision changes, or numbness/tingling

pk: Steady antimycobacterial activity as part of prolonged combination therapy
Plasma peak approximately 1-3 hours after an oral dose
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from moisture
pearls: FDA-approved as Trecator; a second-line thioamide for drug-resistant/MDR-TB, structurally related to isoniazid
Always co-administer pyridoxine to reduce peripheral neuropathy
Watch for hypothyroidism (additive with PAS) and check TSH
Poor GI tolerability is the main limiter - take with food and titrate slowly

missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember, with food. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and continue your usual schedule. Do not double up. Adherence to the full TB regimen is essential to prevent resistance.
overdose: Overdose may intensify GI, neurological, and psychiatric effects. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with attention to liver function, glucose, and CNS status. Pyridoxine may help with neurological symptoms.
